author: Ivan Svetunkov

questions.question: On the M1, M3 and tourism competition data, what were the mean and median RMSSE of CES, and how did they compare with ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method?
questions.answer: Over the 5,315 series of the M1, M3 and tourism data, CES had mean RMSSE 1.959 and median RMSSE 1.170, the lowest of the univariate models: ETS 1.970 and 1.181, ARIMA 2.134 and 1.271, Theta 1.965 and 1.238 (Table 1). The combination SCUM was lower still (1.867 and 1.128).
questions.notes: Must give the CES values and say it was lowest among the univariate models; must not say CES beat SCUM.

questions.question: On the M4 competition data, how did CES compare with ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method on MASE and RMSSE, and were any series left out?
questions.answer: CES had the lowest mean MASE (2.921) and RMSSE (2.339) of the univariate models, and the lowest medians (1.803 and 1.529) (Table 3). Ten series (19357, 43160, 51552, 62738, 92370, 92435, 93159, 93196, 93412, 93491) were excluded because influential outliers and structural breaks made ETS break down.
questions.notes: Must mention the exclusion of 10 series and why. The paper says CES outperforms 'all other models' on MASE and RMSSE, but SCUM and SCUM(noCES) are lower: accept 'lowest of the univariate models'; an answer saying CES beat SCUM is wrong. The ten series numbers are not required.

questions.question: What complex smoothing parameter did CES estimate on M3 series 1664, and what did the authors conclude from it?
questions.answer: α0 + iα1 = 0.99999 + 0.99884i. It satisfies the stationarity condition (11), so the model produces a stationary trajectory: CES identified the series as stationary, in agreement with graphical analysis and the ADF and KPSS tests. The implied ARMA is stationary with long memory, and all holdout observations lay inside the 95% prediction interval.
questions.notes: Must give the value and that it indicates a stationary model. The ARMA values, the agreement with the ADF and KPSS tests and the prediction-interval result are not required.

questions.question: Which single series does the paper discuss as a failure of CES in the M1, M3 and tourism experiment, and how did CES and ETS score on it?
questions.answer: One M1 series (number 47) on which CES failed to identify the trend: its MSIS was 523.034 against 25.590 for ETS. It is the main reason why the mean MSIS of CES is much higher than its median. All models underforecast an unpredictable increase in the holdout, but ETS selected ETS(M,N,N) with a high smoothing parameter (0.881), whose prediction interval exploded and happened to cover it better than the more conservative CES interval.
questions.notes: Must say it is one M1 series on which CES failed to identify the trend and give MSIS 523.034 for CES against 25.590 for ETS. The series number (47) is not required. The explanation of why ETS did better (unpredictable increase, exploding ETS(M,N,N) interval, smoothing parameter 0.881) is not required.

questions.question: Under what condition on the complex smoothing parameter does CES become equivalent to ETS(A,N,N), and how do its parameters then relate to the smoothing parameter of simple exponential smoothing?
questions.answer: When α1 = 1, CES is equivalent to ETS(A,N,N). With α1 close to 1, α0 − 1 in CES corresponds to α in SES (for example α0 = 1.24 corresponds to α = 0.24); α0 near 1 corresponds to a stationary series (SES α near 0) and α0 near 2 to a random walk.
questions.notes: Must give α1 = 1 and α0 − 1 ↔ α. A right answer need not give the example α0 = 1.24.

questions.question: What ARMA model underlies non-seasonal CES, and what are its coefficients?
questions.answer: ARMA(2,2), with φ1 = 2 − α0, φ2 = α0 + α1 − 2, θ1,1 = 2 − 2α0 + α1 and θ1,2 = 3α0 + α1 − 2 − α0² − α1² (equation 17, Appendix B). The AR and MA coefficients are linked through the same two parameters.
questions.notes: Must say ARMA(2,2) and give φ1, φ2, θ1,1 and θ1,2 matching the reference. The coefficients of the second (ξt) equation are not required; if given, accept θ2,1 = −2 + α1 (main text, p. 5) or 2 + α1 (Appendix B), as the paper prints both.

questions.question: Does CES forecast more accurately than the damped trend model ETS(A,Ad,N) on non-seasonal series?
questions.answer: No, not in general. On the 3,262 non-seasonal series (Table 4), ETS(A,Ad,N) has lower mean RMSSE (2.502 vs 2.534), mean and median MASE (2.907 vs 2.949; 1.863 vs 1.880) and mean and median MSIS (3.769 vs 4.269; .854 vs .863); CES is better only on median RMSSE (1.654 vs 1.660). The paper says CES lags behind the damped trend model on mean error measures and is second best in most cases.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says CES beats all ETS models on non-seasonal data.

questions.question: Are the differences in accuracy between CES and ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method on the M1, M3 and tourism data statistically significant?
questions.answer: Not in all cases. In Nemenyi tests at the 5% level CES has the best mean rank of the univariate models on RMSSE and MASE, but the differences are not all statistically significant. SCUM is significantly better than all the other approaches on every measure.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer says CES is significantly better than all univariate benchmarks.

questions.question: Of CES, ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method, does CES have the lowest MSIS (the scaled interval score of the 95% prediction intervals) on the M1, M3 and tourism data and on the M4 data?
questions.answer: Only by the median. On the M1, M3 and tourism data CES has the lowest median MSIS of the univariate models (.869) but the highest mean MSIS (3.465, against 2.258 for ETS). On M4 it again has the lowest median MSIS (.592) but not the lowest mean (2.379, against 2.130 for Theta and 2.272 for ARIMA).
questions.notes: MSIS scores interval width plus a penalty for observations outside the interval; it is not a coverage measure. Overreach if the answer says CES has the lowest MSIS without distinguishing mean and median.

questions.question: Do the paper's results apply to CES with a multiplicative error term?
questions.answer: No. The paper builds CES on an additive error term only; a multiplicative error version is named as future research and is not developed or evaluated.
questions.notes: Overreach if the answer extends the results to multiplicative errors.

questions.question: On seasonal series, does CES outperform every seasonal ETS model on every error measure?
questions.answer: No. On the 2,053 seasonal series (Table 5) CES has the lowest mean and median RMSSE and MASE and the lowest median MSIS, but not the lowest mean MSIS: ETS(M,Md,M) ranks first (1.934 against 2.188 for CES), and ETS(A,N,A), ETS(A,Ad,A) and ETS(M,M,M) are also below CES on mean MSIS.
questions.notes: Must note the mean MSIS exception.

questions.question: What evidence does the paper give that including CES improves the SCUM combination, and is there any measure on which it does not?
questions.answer: SCUM (with CES) is compared with SCUM(noCES). On the M1, M3 and tourism data SCUM has lower mean and median RMSSE and MASE (e.g. mean RMSSE 1.867 vs 1.911) and lower median MSIS, and in Nemenyi tests it is significantly better than every other approach, SCUM(noCES) included. On M4 SCUM is lower on every reported measure. The exception is mean MSIS on the M1, M3 and tourism data, where SCUM (2.333) is worse than SCUM(noCES) (2.223).
questions.notes: Must mention the mean MSIS exception (2.333 against 2.223 on the M1, M3 and tourism data). On Nemenyi ranks SCUM is better on every measure, MSIS included; the exception is in the mean values of Table 1. Accept an answer that gives both.

questions.question: What supports the claim that CES can model both stationary and non-stationary series without a model selection step, and what limitations of this evidence does the paper itself state?
questions.answer: The eigenvalues of the CES transition matrix show that the model is stationary or not depending on α0 and α1 (condition 11; non-stationary when α1 > 1), passing between the two without a switch. Two M3 series illustrate it: on a stationary series (1664) CES estimated a stationary parameter, on a trended one (2721) a non-stationary one. The paper states no limitation of this evidence.
questions.notes: Must give that stationarity depends on α0 and α1 through the eigenvalues of the transition matrix (condition 11) and cite the two M3 examples (series 1664 and 2721). Sources: [p4.17]-[p4.20], [p7.12]-[p7.13], [p8.4]. Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.

questions.question: On what results does the paper base its statement that an information criterion can choose between seasonal and non-seasonal CES, and what limitations of this evidence does the paper itself state?
questions.answer: On the results for the seasonal subset (2,053 series, Table 5): CES, with its seasonal or non-seasonal form chosen automatically by the criterion, beats every seasonal ETS model on RMSSE and MASE. The paper states no limitation of this evidence; it notes only that the split into seasonal and non-seasonal series was made by ETS model selection. (The criterion is called AIC in Sections 3.5 and 4.2 and AICc in Section 4.4.)
questions.notes: Must cite the seasonal-subset results (Table 5) [p11.22]. The RMSSE and MASE details are not required. Accept AIC or AICc. The question is about evidence that the selection works, not about why an information criterion can be computed for CES (the likelihood). The note that the split was made by ETS selection is at [p11.22]; it is not required. Limits: the claimset's limitation objects are the authors' statements too, so a limit given from the claimset is not wrong. Correct: limits stated in the paper or the claimset, or 'none stated' where the paper states none. Wrong: a limit attributed to the paper that neither document states.

questions.question: How is the stability region of CES derived, and is it derived for seasonal CES?
questions.answer: For non-seasonal CES it is derived from the invertibility conditions of the underlying ARMA(2,2), which correspond to stability of the state-space model (Appendix D), giving three inequalities (15): (α0 − 2.5)² + α1² > 1.25, (α0 − 0.5)² + (α1 − 1)² > 0.25 and (α0 − 1.5)² + (α1 − 0.5)² < 1.5. For seasonal CES it is not derived: stability can be checked by requiring all eigenvalues of the discount matrix (21) to lie inside the unit circle; the parameter restrictions are not derived because they cannot be easily analysed.
questions.notes: Must say the seasonal restrictions are not derived. Accept a derivation via the eigenvalues of the discount matrix or via the invertibility of the underlying ARMA(2,2); the paper gives both. The three inequalities need not be written out.
